question: Briefly discuss the chemical pathology of the paediatric patient using the following outline: (a) Introduction, (b) Challenges, (c) Endocrine function, (d) Electrolytes function, (e) Conclusion.
mainConcepts: Age-specific reference intervals and rapid physiological changes in early life
Challenges of small sample volumes, difficult venepuncture and immature homeostatic mechanisms
Endocrine adaptations: thyroid maturation, neonatal hypoglycaemia risk, adrenal function
Electrolyte instability: renal immaturity, sodium/water handling, potassium handling
Implications for test interpretation and clinical decision making in paediatrics
referenceAnswer:
(a) Introduction: Chemical pathology in paediatrics applies biochemical testing to the diagnosis and monitoring of disease in children, with special attention to the physiological and metabolic transitions that occur from birth through infancy.
(b) Challenges: small blood volumes limit repeat testing; difficult venepuncture; no adult reference values apply so age-specific (and sometimes gestation-specific) intervals are required; immature enzyme systems and organ function alter metabolite handling; rapid changes in normal physiology make interpretation difficult.
(c) Endocrine function: neonates are at risk of hypoglycaemia due to immature gluconeogenesis and limited glycogen reserves; thyroid axis matures postnatally (neonatal screening for TSH/T4); adrenal steroidogenesis may be immature; growth and pubertal hormone changes complicate interpretation.
(d) Electrolytes function: renal tubular function is immature at birth, reducing ability to concentrate or dilute urine and to conserve sodium; risk of hyponatraemia (water overload) and hypernatraemic dehydration; potassium handling is immature; fluid requirements per kg body weight are high.
(e) Conclusion: paediatric chemical pathology requires age-appropriate reference intervals, micro-methods, careful sample collection and an understanding of developmental physiology to interpret results safely.

question: (A) 450 blood samples were collected to test for PSA for the diagnosis of prostate cancer. Results: PSA 0-4 ng/mL: True Negative = 130, False Negative = 15. PSA 4-25 ng/mL: True Positive = 270, False Positive = 35. Calculate (a) Sensitivity, (b) Specificity, (c) Positive predictive value, (d) Negative predictive value, (e) overall efficiency. (B) In a tabular form, list two clinical conditions associated with: (i) Vitamin D deficiency, (ii) Elevated GGT, (iii) Magnesium deficiency, (iv) Growth hormone defect, (v) Insulin deficiency, (vi) Proteinuria, (vii) Defect in Phenylalanine metabolism, (viii) Defect in deamination of Leucine, Isoleucine and Valine, (ix) Von Gierke's disease, (x) Mitochondrial disorder.
mainConcepts: Calculating test performance from a 2x2 table
Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN)
Specificity = TN/(TN+FP)
PPV = TP/(TP+FP)
NPV = TN/(TN+FN)
Efficiency = (TP+TN)/(TP+FP+FN+TN)
Clinical conditions illustrating each biochemical abnormality
referenceAnswer:
(A) From the data: TP=270, FP=35, FN=15, TN=130. Total = 450.
(a) Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) = 270/285 = 94.7%
(b) Specificity = TN/(TN+FP) = 130/165 = 78.8%
(c) PPV = TP/(TP+FP) = 270/305 = 88.5%
(d) NPV = TN/(TN+FN) = 130/145 = 89.7%
(e) Efficiency = (TP+TN)/450 = 400/450 = 88.9%
(B) Conditions (two each): (i) Vitamin D deficiency: rickets, osteomalacia. (ii) Elevated GGT: obstructive jaundice, alcohol-related cirrhosis. (iii) Magnesium deficiency: chronic alcoholism, diarrhoea. (iv) Growth hormone defect: pituitary dwarfism, hypopituitarism. (v) Insulin deficiency: type 1 diabetes mellitus, DKA. (vi) Proteinuria: nephrotic syndrome, diabetic nephropathy. (vii) Phenylalanine metabolism defect: phenylketonuria, maternal PKU. (viii) Branch-chain amino acid deamination defect: Maple Syrup Urine Disease. (ix) Von Gierke's disease: glycogen storage disease type 1a (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency), lactic acidosis. (x) Mitochondrial disorder: MELAS, Leigh syndrome.

question: Discuss obesity using the following outline: (a) Epidemiology, (b) Classification, (c) Pathophysiology, (d) Complications.
mainConcepts: Global and local epidemiology of obesity
Classification by BMI and waist circumference
Pathophysiology: energy imbalance, adipocyte dysfunction, leptin resistance, inflammation, insulin resistance
Complications: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, cardiovascular disease, NAFLD, OSA
referenceAnswer:
(a) Epidemiology: obesity is a growing global epidemic affecting adults and increasingly children; rates are highest in Western/urban populations and rising in developing countries including Nigeria, associated with nutrition transition.
(b) Classification: by BMI - overweight 25-29.9 kg/m2; obesity class I 30-34.9; class II 35-39.9; class III (morbid) >=40. Central obesity: waist circumference >102 cm (M) / >88 cm (F).
(c) Pathophysiology: results from chronic positive energy balance (intake > expenditure). Adipose tissue becomes dysfunctional: increased adipocyte size and number, leptin resistance, reduced adiponectin, low-grade chronic inflammation (TNF-alpha, IL-6), ectopic fat deposition, and insulin resistance; genetic (ob gene/leptin, FTO) and environmental factors contribute.
(d) Complications: type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, coronary artery disease, stroke, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, gallstones, osteoarthritis, obstructive sleep apnoea, and reduced life expectancy.

question: Write short notes on: (a) Adrenal hyperfunction, (b) Polycystic ovarian Syndrome (PCOS), (c) List 5 Point of Care Testing devices, their applications and advantages, (d) In a tabular form, differentiate between primary and secondary aldosteronism.
mainConcepts: Adrenal hyperfunction: cortisol (Cushing), aldosterone (Conn), androgens (adrenogenital syndrome)
PCOS: hyperandrogenism, oligo/anovulation, polycystic ovaries on USS, LH/FSH ratio
POCT devices: glucometer, i-STAT, urinalysis strips, pregnancy kits, HbA1c analysers - applications and advantages
Differentiating primary vs secondary aldosteronism by renin levels, cause and response
referenceAnswer:
(a) Adrenal hyperfunction: cortisol excess (Cushing's syndrome - from ACTH-dependent pituitary/ectopic cause or adrenal adenoma, or iatrogenic steroids) presents with central obesity, striae, hypertension and hyperglycaemia. Aldosterone excess (primary hyperaldosteronism/Conn's syndrome) causes hypertension with hypokalaemia, kaliuresis and alkalosis. Androgen excess (adrenogenital syndrome) causes virilisation.
(b) PCOS: common cause of anovulatory infertility. Features: oligomenorrhoea/amenorrhoea, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (acne, hirsutism, raised testosterone), polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, raised LH:FSH ratio (>2-3), insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinaemia, and raised AMH. Managed with weight loss, metformin, ovulation induction and hormonal therapy.
(c) POCT devices (5): Glucometer (glucose monitoring - rapid, near-patient, small volume); i-STAT (blood gases/electrolytes in ICU - portable, cartridges); urine dipstick (proteinuria/glycosuria - cheap, easy); pregnancy test kit (hCG - rapid, no lab required); HbA1c analyser (diabetes monitoring - quick turnaround); plus blood gas analysers, INR/CoaguChek for warfarin monitoring. Advantages: rapid turnaround, reduced sample transport artifacts, convenience and decentralised testing. Limitations: operator dependence and QC concerns.
(d) Primary vs secondary aldosteronism: Primary - aldosterone high, renin suppressed, low PRA, cause = adrenal adenoma/hyperplasia (Conn's), no oedema, normal/high BP, hypokalaemia. Secondary - aldosterone high, renin high/elevated PRA, cause = renal artery stenosis, cardiac failure, cirrhosis, diuretics, pregnancy, with associated oedema or underlying stimulus.
